I can't see the call sites in this hunk, so this is a suspected rather than confirmed bug — worth checking every read of `.definite`.

Moderately confident this at least needs an explicit decision/docs.

For object schemas whose `shape` is a lazy getter (see the `shape` setter immediately above), forcing normalization early can evaluate a self-referential shape and cause stale/partial normalization or infinite recursion for recursive schemas. Additionally, if `cachedInternal` was the only exported variant after a refactor, `util.cached` may no longer exist, which would be a runtime TypeError. I cannot see util.ts in this hunk, so confidence is moderate, but the deliberate `Internal` naming used elsewhere in the same block strongly suggests this is a meaningful semantic difference rather than a rename.

The adjacent singular `property` is kept, so this looks like an unintentional deletion rather than a deliberate API redesign, and no replacement export is added in the hunk. Fairly confident this is at least worth confirming against a changelog/deprecation plan.

rationale: zod mirrors its check exports across `classic` and `mini` and aggregates them in `external.ts`; removing the export from only one place typically breaks the aggregate re-export or leaves the two entrypoints inconsistent. Moderate confidence, contingent on the rest of the repo which isn't visible in this hunk.

Any variant that evaluates earlier (or that memoizes on a shared/internal slot) would eagerly resolve the shape and can cause infinite recursion or stale normalization after `.extend()`/`catchall()` replace the shape. Worth confirming the two helpers have identical laziness semantics; moderate confidence since I could not inspect the helper.

If `cachedInternal` redefines it as `enumerable: false`, any code doing `{ ..._normalized }` or structural comparison/serialization of the normalized holder silently changes result. Low-to-moderate confidence — it depends on the helper's implementation — but it is the most likely intended semantic delta and should be checked against all consumers of `_normalized`.

Previously that snapshot was taken synchronously inside `safeParse`; now it is taken whenever the caller first touches `.error`, which may be much later (or in a different `config()` scope, e.g. after `z.config({ localeError })` or inside a test that resets config in `afterEach`). Now `const r = safeParse(...); if (!r.success) log(r.error)` throws from the property read — code that wrapped only the parse call in try/catch, or that reads `.error` inside a `finally`/logger/serializer, will see an unhandled throw. Previously the raw issues and ctx were dropped as soon as `safeParse` returned. For callers that retain failed results (caches, aggregated validation results over large payloads) this increases retained heap, and the raw `issues` array is aliased from `result.issues`, so any later mutation of that array by the caller would change the lazily-built error. Low confidence this bites, but it is a real difference from the eager version.

If the intent was to drop jsdom 28 support, the code should at least assert the field exists rather than fail silently. Confidence is moderate: I can't rule out that callers never produce `implementation.prototype === mockPrototype`, but if that were guaranteed the original clause would have been dead code, which suggests it was added deliberately. Recommend keeping the `mockPrototype !== parent` check (or wrapping the assignment defensively).

claim: Removing `refCleanupMap.get(container)?.()` means a previously registered ref cleanup is never invoked when the `ref` prop changes or is removed, leaking the old ref/cleanup.
rationale: In the `key === 'ref'` branch, the code proceeds to compute a new `cleanup` and (further down) store it in `refCleanupMap`, overwriting the prior entry. With the invocation removed, the old callback ref never gets called with `null` and its cleanup function becomes unreachable, so listeners/observers registered in the old callback ref leak and stale DOM references are retained. The `value == null` case now performs no cleanup at all. Confidence is moderate-high that this is a regression; it would only be correct if an equivalent cleanup call was added on the caller/unmount path, which is not visible in this hunk.

claim: Removing the HTTP method restriction makes the middleware generate ETags and honor `If-None-Match` for unsafe methods (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), which can turn a mutating request's response into a `304 Not Modified`.
rationale: Previously only GET/HEAD/QUERY reached the ETag logic. With the guard gone, a client that sends `If-None-Match` on a POST whose response body hashes to the same ETag gets a 304 with the body stripped, losing the mutation result. RFC 7232 also says `If-None-Match` on methods other than GET/HEAD should yield 412, not 304. Fairly confident this is a real regression unless a replacement guard exists further down the function (not visible in this hunk).

claim: Removing `!c.res.ok` means error responses (4xx/5xx) and bodyless responses (204/205/304) now get ETags computed and can be converted to 304.
rationale: An error body will now be hashed and an ETag attached; a client repeating the request with that `If-None-Match` receives a 304, which callers interpret as 'unchanged cached success' rather than a repeated error, silently swallowing error semantics. A response that is already 304/204 has no body, so hashing yields an ETag for empty content and may conflict with upstream cache headers. High confidence an explicit status check is still needed.

claim: With both guards gone, every response — including streaming/SSE and very large bodies — now flows into ETag generation, which must buffer the body to hash it.
rationale: ETag generation requires consuming the response body (typically via clone().arrayBuffer() downstream). Previously non-GET and non-ok responses short-circuited; now streamed responses (e.g. SSE from a POST endpoint) and large downloads would be fully buffered, breaking streaming and increasing memory use. Medium confidence — depends on how the code below handles bodyless/stream responses, which isn't shown in this hunk.

claim: `processedSet` is declared inside the per-method loop, so it is re-created on every iteration and can never carry state between handler sets — it is exactly equivalent to the old `!i` test, only with an extra object allocation per iteration (including when `handlerSet` is undefined, on a hot routing path).
rationale: The map is keyed by `handlerSet.score`, which only makes sense if the intent was to remember "this score was already processed" across the outer `for (let i = 0; i < node.#methods.length; i++)` loop. As written the declaration sits inside that loop and is reset each time, so the keying is dead weight. Either the declaration belongs outside the loop (in which case this is a real logic bug — the intended dedup never happens) or the whole map should be dropped in favour of `!i`. Also note the allocation now happens before the `handlerSet !== undefined` check, so it is paid even for methods with no matching handler, which works against the apparent perf goal of this change. Fairly confident this is at minimum wasted work, and likely an intent bug.

claim: Keying the processed flag on `handlerSet.score` rather than on the key index is unsafe if this map is ever hoisted out of the loop: scores are not guaranteed unique across different handler sets.
rationale: `score` is a route-ordering value, and two distinct handler sets matched by the same node can plausibly share a score. If `processedSet` is later moved outside the loop (which is the only way it has any effect), a collision would silently cause the second handler set's first possible key to ignore the incoming `params` and fall back to `nodeParams`, producing wrong path parameters. Flagging as a latent correctness hazard rather than a current bug.

claim: Skipping the key loop when both `nodeParams` and `params` are the shared `emptyParams` sentinel changes observable behavior: previously each `possibleKeys[key]` was explicitly assigned (possibly `undefined`), so the key existed on `handlerSet.params`; now those keys are absent entirely.
rationale: `Object.create(null)` plus no assignments means `'id' in handlerSet.params` is false and `Object.keys(handlerSet.params)` is empty, whereas before both would report the key. Any downstream code that enumerates params or uses `in`/`hasOwnProperty` (e.g. `c.req.param()` returning the full record) would see a different shape. Value-level reads (`params[key]`) still yield `undefined`, so this is only a problem for enumeration/existence checks — but it is a genuine behavior change for existing callers. Medium confidence that something downstream cares.

claim: The guard relies on reference identity with `emptyParams`; any caller that passes a freshly-created empty object, or a `nodeParams` that is empty but not the sentinel, takes the slow path and (more importantly) produces a different `handlerSet.params` shape than the sentinel path.
rationale: Two logically identical inputs (empty params) now yield different results depending on whether the caller happened to reuse the shared sentinel: sentinel → keys absent, other empty object → keys present with `undefined`. That inconsistency is easy to trip over as the codebase evolves. Also note `params` is null-checked (`params && params !== emptyParams`) but `nodeParams` is dereferenced unguarded at line 79 — fine if `nodeParams` is non-optional, but worth confirming against the signature.

claim: `params?.[key] &&` is a truthiness test, so an empty-string path parameter value in `params` is treated as absent and falls through to `nodeParams[key] ?? params?.[key]`.
rationale: Pre-existing behavior that this change preserves rather than introduces, but since the line is being rewritten it is worth deciding deliberately: the correct check for "the incoming params supplied this key" is `params?.[key] !== undefined`. Low impact if empty-string captures are impossible in this matcher, which I could not verify from the hunk alone.

claim: Removing the `try`/`finally` means `this.writer` is never re-acquired when `body.pipeTo(...)` rejects, leaving the StreamingApi permanently without a writer (the writable stays unlocked/errored and `this.writer` still refers to the released writer).
rationale: `this.writer.releaseLock()` is called unconditionally before the pipe. Previously the `finally` block guaranteed `this.writer = this.writable.getWriter()` ran even if `pipeTo` threw (aborted request, source stream error, client disconnect). Now any rejection propagates out of `pipe()` and skips the re-acquire, so any later `write()`/`close()` on the instance will throw `TypeError: Invalid state: The writer is released`, or the object is left in an inconsistent half-piped state. Callers that catch the pipe error and try to continue writing (a common pattern for streaming handlers) will break. High confidence this is a real regression.

claim: Dropping `preventAbort: true` changes error semantics: an error in the source `body` now aborts the destination `this.writable` (the whole response stream) instead of leaving it intact.
rationale: With `preventAbort` unset (default false), `pipeTo` forwards source errors by calling `writable.abort()`, which errors the underlying response stream so nothing further can be written or gracefully closed. Combined with the removed `finally`, `this.writable.getWriter()` on an aborted stream would also yield an errored writer. This is a behavior change for existing callers that relied on the pipe failing in isolation; moderate-to-high confidence it is unintentional since `preventClose` was kept.

claim: `relaxedCookieNameRegEx` is deleted, but the parsing code elsewhere in this file almost certainly still references it, leaving a dangling identifier (TS compile error / ReferenceError at runtime).
rationale: The removed comment explicitly stated the strict regex is "used only when producing cookies via serialize(); parsing uses the relaxed regex below", so a parse()/parseSigned() call site consuming `relaxedCookieNameRegEx` is implied. This hunk removes only the declaration; no corresponding call-site update appears in the diff. If the consumer wasn't updated in another hunk, the module fails to compile. The rest of the file isn't shown, so this needs verification, but it is the most likely breakage here.

claim: Dropping the relaxed name regex reverts cookie-name parsing to the strict RFC 6265 token rule, so incoming cookies whose names contain characters like ':' (e.g. "paraglide:lang") will silently be dropped instead of parsed.
rationale: The removed comments document this exact scenario and link honojs/hono#3189. RFC 6265bis section 5.6 directs consumers to be lenient about names other producers emit in the wild; reinstating the producer-side token rule on the consume path is a silent behavior regression for existing callers - cookies simply disappear from the parse result with no error. Confident this is a real behavior change assuming the parse path now falls back to `validCookieNameRegEx`.

claim: Removing the `jwt?` member drops typed support for API Gateway HTTP API (payload v2) JWT authorizers, a breaking change for any caller reading `requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims` / `.scopes`.
rationale: The runtime event from API Gateway still contains `authorizer.jwt` when a JWT authorizer is configured; only the type declaration is being deleted. Existing user code (and any internal helper that reads JWT claims) will now fail to compile or be forced into `as any` casts, and there is no replacement member or index signature added in this hunk. Unless the property was moved to a v2-specific interface elsewhere in the file (which this hunk does not show), this is a functional regression for JWT-authorizer users. Fairly confident this deserves a second look; severity depends on whether a replacement exists outside the hunk.

claim: Removing `lambda?: Record<string, unknown> | null` removes the only typed path to a REQUEST (Lambda) authorizer's context object for payload format 2.0, so authorizer context becomes inaccessible without casts.
rationale: In payload format 2.0 a Lambda authorizer's returned `context` is nested under `requestContext.authorizer.lambda` (and can legitimately be `null`). With the member gone, callers that relied on `authorizer.lambda` — the documented way to read custom authorizer data — lose type-checked access, and code doing `authorizer.lambda?.userId` will error. The deleted doc comment explicitly described the `null` case, suggesting this was intentional, well-understood behavior that consumers depend on. Moderately confident this is an unintended breaking removal rather than a cleanup of a duplicate declaration.

claim: Removing the `bodyCache.formData` fast path makes `parseFormData` unconditionally call `arrayBuffer()`, which will throw when the request body has already been consumed (e.g. a prior `c.req.formData()` / `c.req.parseBody()` call).
rationale: This guard existed precisely to serve a request whose body was already read and cached as FormData. Without it, the very next line (`await (request as Request).arrayBuffer()`) runs on a disturbed/locked stream and rejects with a TypeError ("Body is unusable" / "Body has already been read"), so any handler that calls `c.req.formData()` before `c.req.parseBody()` (or calls `parseBody` twice, since the code below caches into `bodyCache.formData`) now fails at runtime instead of returning the cached data. It also silently discards a cached FormData that callers may have populated/modified. I'm fairly confident this is a behavior-breaking regression unless the caller was changed to guarantee an unread body.

claim: `arrayBuffer()` is called without consulting `request.bodyCache.arrayBuffer`, so an already-buffered body is not reused.
rationale: Hono's `HonoRequest.bodyCache` also caches `arrayBuffer`; with the FormData short-circuit gone, this path is now the only route and still ignores every cache entry. If `c.req.arrayBuffer()` was called earlier, this throws instead of reusing the cached buffer. Lower confidence (depends on how callers of `parseFormData` are guarded elsewhere), but worth a second look given the guard above was removed.

claim: `#children` now depends on `createNullObject()` preserving the exact semantics of `Object.create(null)`; if the helper returns a shared/cached object or a normal `{}` literal, this silently breaks per-instance isolation or prototype-pollution safety.
rationale: This field initializer runs once per `Node` instance and the router mutates `#children` by arbitrary path-segment keys. Two failure modes are plausible and not visible in this hunk: (a) if `createNullObject` returns a module-level singleton (a common shape for such a helper, e.g. `const NULL_OBJ = Object.create(null); export const createNullObject = () => NULL_OBJ`), every Node would share one children map and routing would be completely wrong; (b) if it returns `{}` or `Object.assign({}, ...)` rather than a null-prototype object, then route segments named `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, etc. would hit inherited properties — the `node.#children[token]` lookups would return `Object.prototype` members instead of `undefined`, and `__proto__` assignment would be swallowed. The original `Object.create(null)` was almost certainly deliberate for exactly this reason. Medium confidence that there is a real bug (depends on the unseen helper), high confidence this is worth verifying.

claim: The declared type `Record<string, Node>` may no longer be checked if `createNullObject()` returns `any`.
rationale: `Object.create(null)` returns `any` in TypeScript, so the annotation was the only thing giving this field a type; a wrapper that also returns `any` (rather than a generic `createNullObject<T>(): T` or `Record<string, never>`) keeps the same weak-typing hole, and a wrapper returning something narrower (e.g. `Record<string, unknown>`) would fail to assign here. Low-to-medium confidence; worth confirming the helper is generic so the annotation still carries weight.

claim: The new `jsonContentTypeRegex` only accepts `application/...` media types, so JSON responses served as `text/json`, `text/x-json`, or any `text/...+json` subtype will no longer be pretty-printed.
rationale: The regex is anchored with `^application\/`. If the previous implementation used a looser check (e.g. `includes('application/json')` or a check that also tolerated other types), this is a silent behavior change for callers that set a non-`application` JSON content type. Medium confidence, since the call site isn't shown in the hunk, but the anchor is clearly restrictive.

claim: The trailing lookahead `(?=$|[;\s])` rejects a comma, so a combined/duplicated header value such as `application/json,application/json` (which fetch/Headers produces when the header is appended twice) will not be recognized as JSON.
rationale: `Headers.get()` joins repeated header values with `, `. With `application/json, application/json` the first value ends with `,`, which is neither end-of-string, `;`, nor whitespace, so the match fails and prettification is skipped. Low-to-medium likelihood in practice but a real edge case; adding `,` to the lookahead character class would cover it.

claim: The structured-suffix subtype pattern `[a-z0-9._-]+\+` does not allow `+` inside the subtype prefix, so media types with more than one suffix segment (e.g. `application/vnd.foo+xml+json`) or subtypes containing other token characters permitted by RFC 6838 (`!#$&^`, etc.) are not matched.
rationale: RFC 6838 restricted-name characters are broader than `[a-z0-9._-]`. This is a narrow edge case and unlikely to matter for real-world APIs, but it means some legitimately JSON-suffixed types are skipped. Low confidence that it matters in practice.

claim: The regex does not tolerate leading whitespace in the header value (e.g. `" application/json"`), since it is anchored at `^`.
rationale: Header values are normally trimmed by the HTTP stack/Headers implementation, so this is mostly theoretical, but if the value is set manually via `c.header('Content-Type', ' application/json')` the check silently fails. Low confidence this is reachable.

claim: The new head fast-path duplicates the matching predicate but is not exactly equivalent to it: it adds a `!isNodeString(first)` guard that the `findIndex` predicate does not have.
rationale: In the original, for a non-string `child` with no key the predicate is `(c) => c.tag === (child as Node).tag`, which would also match a `NodeString` element whose `tag` is `undefined` if `child.tag` were ever `undefined` (e.g. a node with an undefined/falsy tag). The fast path short-circuits those cases to `false` and falls through to the scan, which will re-test index 0 and reach the same result, so in practice behaviour is probably identical — my main concern is that the same matching rule now exists in two textual copies that can silently drift apart on a future edit (and the fast path is the one that wins). Medium confidence that this is only a maintainability/perf redundancy rather than a live bug.

claim: `oldVChildren.shift()` (like the previous `splice`) removes the node from the array but not from `oldChildrenByKey`, so once the index has been built a node can be consumed twice.
rationale: The keyed branch above (`oldChildrenByKey.delete(key)`) consumes nodes from the map without removing them from `oldVChildren`, and this branch consumes from `oldVChildren` without deleting from the map. After `indexChildrenByKey(oldVChildren)` has run, an unkeyed child hitting this branch can now claim the head node even if it was already reused via the key map (and vice versa), which would reuse the same DOM node for two children. This desync is pre-existing, but the new `shift()` fast path makes claiming the stale head the cheapest/most likely outcome, so it is worth re-checking whether the two consumption paths stay in sync. Moderate confidence — depends on the exact condition of the `if` branch above, which is not fully visible here.

claim: The `scanBudget < 0` / indexing fallback is now nested inside the `else` branch, so it is skipped whenever the head matches.
rationale: This is likely intentional (a head match costs zero scan, so the budget cannot newly go negative there), and `scanBudget` is set to `Infinity` as soon as indexing happens, so it cannot be left negative across iterations. Flagging only so the author confirms there is no path where `scanBudget` is already negative on entry and the head happens to match, which would defer index construction indefinitely. Low confidence that this is an actual defect.

claim: The newly added `chUaHighEntropyValues` does not correspond to any known Permissions-Policy / Client Hints feature token; the camelCase-to-kebab serialization would emit `ch-ua-high-entropy-values`, which browsers will ignore as an unrecognized policy.
rationale: The standardized client-hint policy-controlled features are `ch-ua`, `ch-ua-arch`, `ch-ua-bitness`, `ch-ua-form-factors`, `ch-ua-full-version`, `ch-ua-full-version-list`, `ch-ua-mobile`, `ch-ua-model`, `ch-ua-platform`, `ch-ua-platform-version`, `ch-ua-wow64`. "High entropy values" is the name of the `navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues()` API, not a delegatable hint token — there is no `Sec-CH-UA-High-Entropy-Values` header. Exposing this in the public `StandardizedFeatures` type invites callers to emit a directive that silently does nothing. Medium confidence; if a feature really was missing from this list, `chUaFormFactors` is the likely intended one.

claim: Adding a member to `StandardizedFeatures` may require a matching entry in any runtime mapping/allow-list (and its tests/docs) that consumes this type.
rationale: Only the type declaration is visible in this hunk. If the header is built via a generic camelCase→kebab transform this is fine, but if there is a non-exhaustive lookup object (e.g. `Partial<Record<StandardizedFeatures, string>>` or a plain object literal), the new key would serialize to `undefined` or be dropped at runtime with no compile error. Low-to-medium confidence since the implementation isn't shown.

claim: Hoisting `allowHeadersStr` out of the request handler can break the per-request fallback to the incoming `Access-Control-Request-Headers` header.
rationale: In typical CORS middleware implementations (including Hono's), when `opts.allowHeaders` is empty the preflight response echoes the request's `Access-Control-Request-Headers` value, which is inherently per-request. Computing a single `allowHeadersStr` at middleware-construction time is only safe if the handler still keeps that dynamic branch; if the handler was refactored to just use `allowHeadersStr`, preflight responses will silently stop advertising the requested headers. I can't see the handler body in this hunk, so this is a suspicion worth verifying at the usage site.

claim: Caching the joined header strings freezes the values, changing behavior if the caller mutates the arrays passed in `options` after `cors()` is called.
rationale: Previously the `join(',')` presumably happened per request, so pushing to the array reference the caller supplied (e.g. `const headers = []; app.use(cors({ allowHeaders: headers })); headers.push('X-Foo')`) would be reflected. Now the strings are computed once at setup. Unusual but plausible usage; the change is silent. Moderate-low confidence anyone relies on it.

claim: `?.length` collapses both "empty array" and "undefined" into `undefined`, losing the distinction of an explicitly empty allow/expose list.
rationale: Defaults set `allowHeaders: []` / `exposeHeaders: []`, and a caller can also pass `{ exposeHeaders: undefined }` via the spread. With this change no `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` header is emitted for an empty list. That matches old behavior only if the previous handler also guarded on `.length`; if it unconditionally joined and set the header, this changes an empty-valued header into an absent header. Worth confirming against the original handler code.

claim: The new branch returns a non-zero result when `a` and `b` are the same wildcard string, making the comparator non-reflexive/asymmetric (compareKey(TAIL, TAIL) === -1 and compareKey(ONLY, ONLY) === 1).
rationale: With `a === TAIL_WILDCARD_REG_EXP_STR` and `b === TAIL_WILDCARD_REG_EXP_STR`, the ternary yields -1; symmetrically the reversed call also yields -1, which violates the contract that equal elements compare to 0. Likewise two `ONLY_WILDCARD` keys both yield 1. In practice this may be harmless if the caller only sorts unique object keys or short-circuits on `a === b` earlier in the function (the top of the function isn't shown), but if that guard doesn't exist the sort order becomes implementation-defined/unstable. Medium-low confidence that it is reachable; worth a guard such as `if (a === b) return 0` before the wildcard block.

claim: Behavior change: the only-wildcard (`.*`) no longer always sorts last, which reorders route matching priority relative to the tail wildcard.
rationale: Previously any wildcard key compared as greater than everything else, so `.*` and the tail wildcard were ordered only by the fallback/stable-sort behavior. Now `.*` is explicitly placed before the tail wildcard. This changes the generated RegExp alternation order and therefore which route wins for paths matched by both `/foo/*` style and tail-wildcard patterns. Assuming this is the intent of the change, but existing callers relying on the old precedence (e.g. `/:x/*` vs `/:x` tail behavior) could see different matches; worth covering with a test for a route set containing both wildcard forms at the same node.

claim: `Accept-Query` is added only to the `RequestHeader` type union; if the module has a parallel runtime list (e.g. an exported `const requestHeaders = [...] as const`, a validation Set, or a matching `ResponseHeader` union), those will now be out of sync with the type.
rationale: Only this one hunk is shown, so I cannot verify whether a runtime array or a sibling union exists in the same file. Hand-maintained header lists in TS very often have both a type union and a runtime `as const` array (or a separate ResponseHeader union), and adding to one without the other silently breaks lookups/validation at runtime while type-checking passes. Worth confirming the rest of headers.ts. Low-to-moderate confidence since the file content outside the hunk is unknown.

claim: `Accept-Query` (RFC 9727) is defined as a *response* header advertising the query formats a resource accepts for the QUERY method, not a request header, so listing it under `RequestHeader` may be semantically wrong.
rationale: Per RFC 9727, `Accept-Query` is sent by the server in a response (typically to OPTIONS) to indicate supported QUERY content types. The surrounding union does already mix in response-only names such as `Accept-Patch`, `Accept-Post`, `Accept-Ranges`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, so this file may intentionally be a combined list — in which case this is a non-issue. Flagging so the author can confirm the union's intended semantics; moderate confidence about the RFC, low confidence that it matters here.

claim: The new `@param {string} [options.realm]` doc claims the default is "the request URL" — this must be verified against the actual implementation (and against the sibling `jwt` middleware, whose `WWW-Authenticate` realm defaults to `ctx.req.url`). If the implementation instead defaults to an empty string or omits the parameter when unset, the documentation is misleading for callers relying on the documented fallback.
rationale: The hunk only adds documentation; the corresponding option type and the code emitting the `WWW-Authenticate` header are not shown, so the documented default cannot be confirmed here. Moderate confidence this needs cross-checking; documentation drift on an auth-related header is easy for callers to trip over.

claim: A caller-supplied `realm` string is interpolated into the `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="..."` challenge; if the implementation does not escape/validate double quotes, backslashes, CR/LF or non-ASCII characters, a realm value can break out of the quoted-string or inject additional auth-param/header content.
rationale: RFC 7235 quoted-string values require escaping of `"` and `\`, and header values must not contain CR/LF. Since this option is newly exposed to users, the sanitization path should be checked. Low-to-moderate confidence because the implementation is outside this hunk, but the risk is concrete if unhandled.

claim: Unlike `keys` and `jwks_uri`, `realm` is documented as only `string` rather than also accepting a `(ctx: Context) => string | Promise<string>` resolver.
rationale: Callers commonly want a per-request/per-tenant realm; the inconsistency with the other options may be intentional, but it is worth confirming that the declared type matches the option type actually accepted, otherwise the docs and the type will disagree. Low confidence — this may simply be a deliberate API choice.

claim: The documented default for `options.allowMethods` now advertises `'QUERY'`, which must match the actual default array in the `cors()` implementation; if the runtime default was not also updated, the docs describe behavior that does not exist.
rationale: This hunk only touches the JSDoc block, not the code that builds the default `allowMethods`. I cannot see the implementation body in the provided context, so I cannot confirm the runtime default includes 'QUERY'. If it does not, callers reading the docs will assume preflight requests for the QUERY method are permitted by default and will hit an unexpected CORS failure. Conversely, if the implementation was updated in another hunk, adding 'QUERY' to the default `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` is a behavior change for existing callers relying on the previous narrower default and should be called out in release notes. Low-to-moderate confidence that an actual mismatch exists; flagged for verification.

claim: `cloneRawRequest` is a new *value* import from `../../request` inside a middleware module, turning what was a type-only dependency graph into a runtime one and risking a circular import (`request` → `context`/`types` → middleware barrels).
rationale: Previously this file imported only `type`-level symbols, so it had zero runtime coupling to the core. A runtime import of `../../request` can create an import cycle (and, in bundlers/ESM, a temporarily-undefined binding at module-evaluation time) depending on what `request.ts` pulls in. Medium-low confidence without seeing the full module graph, but it is a real hazard worth verifying, e.g. by checking that `src/request.ts` does not transitively import this middleware and that the helper is actually exported there.

claim: `sha256` from `../../utils/crypto` resolves to `Promise<string | null>` in Hono, but the new `CacheKeyRequest` type declares `digest: string` — the null/unavailable-WebCrypto case appears unhandled.
rationale: Hono's `sha256` returns `null` when `crypto.subtle` is missing or digesting fails. If that value is assigned into `digest: string` (via a non-null assertion or implicit cast) every request in such a runtime collapses to the same digest, so different QUERY bodies would share one cache key — a correctness/cache-poisoning bug, not just a type nit. Also note `sha256` is async, so any code path building the cache key must be awaited. High confidence that the type is too narrow; medium confidence about how the call site handles it since it is outside this hunk.

claim: The reserved cache-key query parameters (`__hono_cache_key`, `__hono_cache_method`, `__hono_query_digest`, `__hono_cache_vary`) are not namespaced against client-supplied query strings, so a request whose own URL already contains one of these names can collide with or forge another entry's cache key.
rationale: If the synthetic key URL is built by appending these parameters to (or embedding) the original URL/query, a client sending `?__hono_query_digest=<x>` or `?__hono_cache_vary=...` can make two semantically different requests map to the same key, or make a GET request masquerade as a QUERY entry. That is cache poisoning / cross-response leakage. The fix is to strip or reject these parameters from the incoming URL before constructing the key, or to encode the original URL opaquely (e.g. as a single digested value) rather than concatenating. Medium confidence — depends on the construction code not shown — but the naming convention alone gives no protection.

claim: `defaultMaxQueryBodySize = 64 * 1024` introduces a hard-coded body-size cutoff; behavior at the boundary (truncate-and-digest vs. bypass cache) is safety-critical and the constant gives no indication which is intended.
rationale: If oversized bodies are truncated before digesting, two different large QUERY bodies sharing their first 64 KiB would produce identical cache keys and serve each other's responses. The only safe behavior is to skip caching entirely once the limit is exceeded. Also worth confirming the comparison uses `>` on the actual byte length (not `>=`, and not `Content-Length`, which can be absent or lie for streamed bodies). Low-to-medium confidence since the usage is outside this hunk, but the failure mode is severe enough to verify.

claim: `queryRepresentationMetadataHeaders` omits `content-length`, and the fixed lowercase list is only safe if lookups go through `Headers.get`.
rationale: Per RFC 9110 the representation metadata for a QUERY payload also includes `Content-Length`; excluding it is probably harmless because the digest covers the body bytes, but if the digest is computed over a *stream* rather than the full buffer, a length mismatch could go undetected. Additionally, if these names are ever matched against raw header keys (e.g. iterating a plain object of headers) instead of `Headers.get`, the lowercase-only list will silently miss `Content-Type`. Low confidence — mostly a prompt to double-check the consumer of this list.

claim: Adding `QUERY` only to the `If-None-Match: *` branch leaves the two branches inconsistent: the non-`*` branch (`etagMatches`) applies to any method, so the method gate is only ever enforced for `*`.
rationale: Per RFC 9110 §13.1.2 an `If-None-Match` that evaluates to false should yield 304 only for GET/HEAD (and now arguably QUERY, which is defined as safe/cacheable) and 412 otherwise. This middleware already ignores the method in the `etagMatches` path, and the change widens only the `*` path, so a POST/PUT with a matching concrete ETag still gets a 304 while `*` does not. Medium confidence this is intentional-but-incomplete rather than an outright bug, but worth a look while the method list is being touched.

claim: Method is compared against hardcoded, case-sensitive literals and the "safe/cacheable method" list is duplicated inline rather than shared, so other method-gated logic may not have been updated for QUERY.
rationale: `c.req.method` comes verbatim from the incoming Request, so a lowercase `query` would not match (same pre-existing limitation as GET/HEAD, so low risk). The bigger concern is that if other places (cache middleware, conditional-request helpers, body-handling for 304) also gate on `GET || HEAD`, they were not updated here, leaving QUERY handled inconsistently. Low-to-medium confidence since only this hunk is visible.

claim: Returning a bodyless 304 for a QUERY request may not be handled by all clients/intermediaries, since QUERY carries a request body and its caching semantics are still draft-stage.
rationale: The QUERY method spec is not yet a finalized RFC; treating it as cache-revalidatable by default changes behavior for any existing caller that sends `If-None-Match: *` with QUERY and currently receives a full 200 response. Low confidence this is a real problem, but it is a user-visible behavior change that is not gated by any option.

claim: Initializing `env` to `{}` is an unsafe default for the generic type `E['Bindings']`, which may be a concrete non-empty binding type.
rationale: `E['Bindings']` is resolved from the user's Env generic (e.g. `{ COUNTER: DurableObjectNamespace }`). `{}` is not structurally assignable to such a type, so this either requires a cast/`as unknown as` to compile or silently lies about the runtime shape: `c.env.COUNTER` is typed as present but is `undefined`. Previously the field was simply uninitialized, which was equally undefined at runtime but at least didn't claim a valid value existed. Fairly confident this is a typing concern; whether it compiles depends on the declared constraint on `Bindings`.

claim: The `{}` default is likely clobbered back to `undefined` by the constructor when `options` is provided but `options.env` is not.
rationale: Context's constructor typically does `if (options) { this.env = options.env; ... }` unconditionally. Class field initializers run before the constructor body, so for any Context created with an options object lacking `env` (a very common path in tests and in non-workers runtimes), `this.env` is reassigned to `undefined` and the new default never takes effect. If the intent is a guaranteed non-null `env`, the assignment needs to be guarded (e.g. `if (options.env) this.env = options.env`). Confidence is moderate since the constructor isn't shown in this hunk — worth verifying.

claim: Behavior change: `c.env` is now truthy/non-null by default, breaking existing `if (!c.env)` / `c.env ?? fallback` guards in user and middleware code.
rationale: Callers commonly branch on whether bindings exist (e.g. to distinguish Workers from Node/Deno runtimes, or to fall back to `process.env`). With a `{}` default those guards stop firing and property access yields `undefined` deeper in the call chain instead, turning an early, explicit check into a later, less obvious failure. This is a real observable semantic change for existing consumers.

claim: Adding an object-literal field initializer allocates a fresh object on every Context construction, adding per-request overhead.
rationale: A Context is created for every request in a hot path; the previous uninitialized field cost nothing, whereas `= {}` allocates a new empty object per instance even when it is immediately overwritten by `options.env`. In a framework where per-request allocations are deliberately minimized this is a measurable (if small) regression; a shared frozen empty-object constant would avoid it.

claim: Removing the `done` check means a prematurely closed/ended stream no longer produces the explicit `Stream closed unexpectedly` error; instead `value` is `undefined` and the array destructuring throws an opaque `TypeError: undefined is not iterable`.
rationale: `ReadableStreamDefaultReader.read()` resolves with `{ done: true, value: undefined }` when the stream ends. Line 557 destructures `value` unconditionally, so when the producer closes the stream (network drop, aborted request, malformed payload) the consumer now surfaces a confusing TypeError instead of the intentional domain error, and any caller matching on that message will break. Also, if the reject branch relied on the guaranteed-present chunk, downstream promise rejection semantics change. High confidence this is a real behavior regression unless the caller guarantees the stream can never close here — which is exactly what the removed guard was defending against.

claim: `value as PromiseChunk` is now an unsound cast: without the `done` guard, `value`'s actual type includes `undefined`.
rationale: Previously the `if (done) throw` narrowed `value` to the non-undefined branch before the cast, so the assertion was safe. After the change the cast silently launders `undefined` into `PromiseChunk`, defeating the type checker at the exact spot where the runtime failure occurs. Medium-high confidence; depends on how the reader's read() result is typed in this codebase.

claim: `raceAbortSignals` is dropped from the imports; if any remaining code in this file still references it the module will fail to compile, and if the call site was removed as part of this change it silently drops per-request abort-signal racing.
rationale: The hunk only shows the import list, so I cannot see the body of httpBatchLink.ts. In the current tRPC batch link, `raceAbortSignals` is normally used to combine the batch's aggregate signal (`allAbortSignals`) with a per-request/abort-on-unmount signal so the in-flight fetch is cancelled when either fires. Removing the import means either (a) a dangling reference remains -> TS2304 build break, or (b) the racing behaviour was deleted, which changes cancellation semantics: the HTTP request would now only abort when *all* batched callers abort (allAbortSignals), never when an individual one does. Both outcomes are worth verifying. Medium confidence, since the rest of the file isn't visible in this hunk.

claim: Removing `clientSubscriptions.delete(id)` from the subscription error handler leaves the failed subscription registered in the map forever, while the success path (line 407) still deletes it — an asymmetric cleanup that leaks entries and can break reuse of the same request id.
rationale: In the tRPC ws adapter, `clientSubscriptions` maps a JSON-RPC request id to the subscription's abort controller and is used (a) to reject/ignore a new `subscription` message that reuses an already-registered id, (b) to handle `subscription.stop`, and (c) to abort everything on socket close. If the entry is never removed when the subscription errors, then: the client can never re-subscribe with that id (it will be treated as a duplicate), a later `subscription.stop` for that id acts on an already-dead subscription, and the controller stays reachable until the connection closes — a per-connection memory leak that grows with every failed subscription. The delete is still performed on the normal completion path just above, so the two paths are now inconsistent. This is only safe if the same deletion was moved into a `.finally()`, an abort/close listener, or the `catch` block further down (outside this hunk); if so, this is a no-op refactor. Since I can't see the surrounding code, I'd verify that an equivalent cleanup exists on the error path before accepting the removal. Confidence that this is a real regression: moderate.

rationale: The `input` is only retained inside `getQueryKeyInternal({ ... input: arg1 ... })`, which is used solely to build the cache/query key. Unless `trpcSubscriptionOptions` derives the input from `queryKey` (e.g. `queryKey[0][1].input`), the subscription will be invoked with `undefined` input while still being keyed by the input — producing a silently wrong request (and possibly an input-validation error server-side). This is a behavior change for every existing caller of `subscriptionOptions(input)`. Moderately confident this is a bug; it is only safe if `trpcSubscriptionOptions` was simultaneously changed to read the input out of `queryKey`, and even then the two sources could diverge.

claim: Removing the `onAbort` registration drops the abort→`observer.complete()` behavior, so an aborted signal may no longer terminate the observable (and an already-aborted signal is no longer handled synchronously).
rationale: Previously, aborting the AbortSignal completed the observer, which is what triggers teardown (and the `subscription.stop` send). With this block deleted, unless an equivalent `signal.addEventListener('abort', abort, ...)` was added elsewhere in the function (not visible in this hunk), an abort will never complete the observable: the consumer hangs, the teardown never runs, and the server-side subscription is never stopped. The `signal?.aborted` fast path is also gone, so subscribing with an already-aborted signal now starts the request instead of completing immediately. Confident this is a real behavior change unless the listener was moved above the hunk; worth verifying.

claim: `removeEventListener('abort', abort)` references a different function than whatever was registered; if `abort` was never added as an abort listener this is a silent no-op leak.
rationale: removeEventListener only removes a listener registered with the exact same function reference. The corresponding `addEventListener` call was deleted in this same hunk, so as written this line can only work if `abort` is registered as the 'abort' listener elsewhere in the function. If it is not, the call does nothing (harmless but misleading); if it is registered but wrapped (e.g. `() => abort()`), the listener is never removed and the signal keeps a strong reference to the closure, leaking per-subscription state on long-lived signals. Additionally, used as a listener, `abort` would be invoked with an Event argument — check that `abort`'s signature tolerates that.

claim: The rewritten condition only rejects `NaN`; all other invalid request-id values (undefined, booleans, objects, arrays, functions) now pass the assertion and are unsoundly typed as `number | string | null`.

Because `typeof obj === 'number'` is required, the only value satisfying every conjunct is `NaN`. The previous predicate threw for anything that was not null / string / finite-or-infinite number. This is a clear validation regression on untrusted wire input parsed by the RPC message parser, and the `asserts obj is number | string | null` signature makes it a lie to all downstream callers. High confidence.

It is a strong signal the refactor of the boolean expression was mechanical rather than semantics-preserving. High confidence this clause is redundant as written.

Fairly confident this is a real behavior change unless `prefix` was already unused inside `trpcMutationOptions`.

Even if the intent was to stop prefixing mutations, this is an observable cross-cutting behavior change that deserves a test and a changeset note. Moderate confidence.

rationale: Previously `accessor` was textually inlined three times inside one loop header/body that the author controlled. The new comment says the body runs "once per string key and once per symbol key", which implies `emitOwnKeys` emits two loops, so the `accessor` expression is likely spliced into more emitted sites than before. If `accessor` is a non-trivial expression (e.g. a property chain or a call with getters), duplicating it changes evaluation count/cost and can observe getters multiple times. Worth confirming that `accessor` is always a simple variable reference at this call site, or that the helper caches it in a local.

rationale: `newVar(ctx)` is called once, but the emitted body containing `let ${outKeyVar} = ...` is now produced by the callback passed to `emitOwnKeys`. If the helper invokes the callback twice (once for the string-key loop, once for the symbol-key loop) within the *same* block scope rather than two separate `{ ... }` blocks, the generated code would contain a duplicate `let` declaration for the same identifier and throw a SyntaxError at codegen-eval time. This is only safe if each loop body is its own block; worth verifying.

rationale: The retry line is guarded by `typeof ${kVar} === "string"`, so it is safe for symbols, but if `emitOwnKeys` specializes the string loop and symbol loop separately, this guard becomes dead code in one branch and the symbol branch still pays for the emitted check. Low impact, but if the helper instead narrows `kVar` typing assumptions (e.g. emits `String(k)` coercion in the symbol loop), the `typeof === "string"` guard could misfire and attempt `Number(symbolKey)`, which throws. Confidence low; flagging for a read of the helper.

claim: The effect dependency array was changed from `[subscribe]` to `[]`, so the store is never re-subscribed when `subscribe` (or `getSnapshot`) identity changes.
rationale: `useSyncExternalStore` is specified to resubscribe when `subscribe` changes (React uses `[subscribe, getSnapshot]`). With `[]`, a component that switches to a different store instance, or whose `subscribe` closure captures new props, keeps listening to the stale store forever and silently stops receiving updates. The removed comment above the old effect shows the previous code deliberately handled the swap. High confidence this is a real regression.

claim: The `Object.is(snapshot, getSnapshot())` re-check is now only performed when the server snapshot was used, so client-side store mutations between the initial render and the effect flush are lost.
rationale: The new effect does `if (serverSnapshotIsUsed) setState(getSnapshot())` before subscribing. On the pure client path (`serverSnapshotIsUsed === false`) nothing re-reads the store, so any change that happens after `useState`'s lazy initializer ran but before `subscribe` was called is missed, and the component stays stale until the next unrelated store event. The old code covered this case unconditionally. Fairly confident.

claim: The snapshot is no longer re-read on every render; the component now returns a `useState` value that only advances via the subscription callback, which can tear on renders triggered by other sources.
rationale: Previously `getSnapshot()` was invoked each render, so any parent-triggered re-render produced a fresh, consistent snapshot. Now a re-render caused by props/other state returns the cached `state`, which may be older than the store's current value until a subscription notification arrives. This is exactly the tearing that `useSyncExternalStore` exists to prevent. Medium-high confidence depending on how Hono schedules subscription updates.

claim: `setState(getSnapshot())` will be misinterpreted as a functional updater if the snapshot value is itself a function.
rationale: Hono's `useState` setter, like React's, treats a function argument as `(prev) => next`. A store whose snapshot is a function (e.g. a selector or callback store) would have the function invoked with the previous snapshot instead of being stored. The old code used a `setVersion((v) => v + 1)` counter and read the snapshot during render, so it was immune. Niche but concrete edge case; the fix is `setState(() => getSnapshot())`.

claim: The subscription callback closes over the first-render `getSnapshot`, which is never refreshed, so updates can read from a stale snapshot getter.
rationale: Because the effect runs only once (`[]` deps), the `getSnapshot` captured in `subscribe(() => setState(getSnapshot()))` is permanently the one from the initial render. `getSnapshot` is very often an inline closure over props, so later notifications would produce values derived from stale props. Related to but distinct from the missing `subscribe` dep: even re-subscribing on `subscribe` alone would not fix it. Confident this is a latent bug.

claim: `serverSnapshotIsUsed` is stored via `useState` with a non-lazy initializer, so `buildData[0][4] && getServerSnapshot` is evaluated on every render even though only the first value is kept.
rationale: Functionally harmless for the boolean itself, but it means `getServerSnapshot`'s presence/absence on later renders is ignored, and the expression cost is paid each render. Worth a second look mainly because the frozen-on-mount semantics differ from the previous per-render check of `buildData[0][4]`; if a component can be rendered once on the server and then hydrated through the same hook state, the frozen value could be wrong. Low-medium confidence that this matters in practice.
